headline: Giant bluefin crash the 100-fathom line as warm eddies spin off the Stream
subhead: Chunking and trolling both producing as temperature breaks stack bait along the canyon walls.
body_markdown:
The canyon is absolutely on fire right now, with giant bluefin tuna showing up in numbers I haven't seen in years. We're talking fish in the 90-inch class crashing chunks and trolling spreads along the 100-fathom line, where a beautiful warm-water eddy has spun off the Gulf Stream and set up shop.

The action started building last week when I noticed the temperature break sharpening up between the canyon wall and the deeper water. What we've got now is a classic setup — 72-degree blue water sitting right against 68-degree green water, creating that edge where everything stacks up. The bait is thick in there, mostly adult bunker with some good-sized mackerel mixed in, and the tuna are absolutely demolishing them.

Chunking has been the go-to technique for the biggest fish. I'm running out to the 30-fathom line on the western wall where the eddy pushes right up against the shelf. Fresh bunker chunks, thumb-sized, on 8/0 circles with 80-pound fluorocarbon leaders. The key is getting your drift right — you want to be drifting with the current along that temperature break, not across it. I've been starting my drift uptide of the break and letting it carry me right down the edge.

The bite window has been pretty consistent — first light through about 10 AM, then again from 4 PM until dark. These fish are feeding aggressively, and when they're on the chunk, they're not shy about it. I had one morning last week where we hooked five fish over 80 inches in two hours, all on the same drift line.

Trolling is producing too, especially for the guys who want to cover more water. The spread that's been working is a mix of cedar plugs and ballyhoo. I'm running two cedar plugs on the long riggers — one natural, one blue and white — and ballyhoo on the short riggers and flat lines. Speed is critical — these fish want it fast, around 8 to 9 knots. Any slower and you're missing bites.

The wahoo have been a nice bonus fish on the troll. They're hitting the same cedar plugs that are taking tuna, mostly in the 30 to 40-pound class. I've also picked up some nice mahi in the 15 to 25-pound range, particularly around any floating debris or weed lines you can find in that warm water.

What's really exciting is the white marlin activity. I've been seeing good numbers of fish in the spread, and while the bite has been a little finicky, the fish are there. They seem to prefer the ballyhoo over the cedar plugs, and I've had the best luck running them on the flat lines with no weight, just swimming naturally behind the boat.

The key to this whole bite is understanding how that eddy is positioned. It's not a static thing — it moves and shifts with the current and wind. I've been watching the water color closely and using my surface temperature gauge to find where that break is setting up each day. Some days it's tight to the 100-fathom line, other days it pushes in to 80 fathoms or slides out to 120.

Bait has been easy to find. The bunker schools are thick along the temperature break, and I've been catching all the chunk bait I need with a sabiki rig in 60 to 80 feet of water. The mackerel are there too, though they're a little deeper, usually in 100 to 120 feet.

Looking ahead, this setup should hold for at least another week, maybe longer if the eddy stays put. The new moon is coming up this weekend, which should get the current moving and potentially tighten up that temperature break even more. I'm expecting the bite to stay strong, especially on the chunk. If you're planning a trip out here, bring plenty of bunker and don't be afraid to fish heavy — these fish are not playing around.
